By Jacob Rivera, Creative Director at The Ultimate Snooze

Of all the supplements marketed for sleep, magnesium has some of the most legitimate mechanistic support. Unlike melatonin — which is a timing hormone often used incorrectly — magnesium operates directly on the nervous system pathways involved in relaxation and sleep induction. Understanding how it works and which form to take is worth a few minutes if sleep quality is a priority.

Why Magnesium Matters for Sleep

Magnesium is the fourth most abundant mineral in the human body and a cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions. For sleep specifically, two mechanisms are most relevant.

GABA receptor activation: Magnesium binds to and activates GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) receptors in the brain. GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter — it quiets neural activity and promotes the calm, reduced arousal state that precedes sleep. This is the same receptor family targeted by benzodiazepine sleep medications and alcohol, which is why low magnesium status is associated with anxiety, hyperarousal, and difficulty falling asleep.

NMDA receptor blockade: Magnesium blocks NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors, which are involved in excitatory neural activity. By reducing excitatory signaling and enhancing inhibitory signaling simultaneously, magnesium creates a dual effect that supports the transition from the active, alert nervous system state to the calm, sleep-ready state.

Research published in the Journal of Research in Medical Sciences found that magnesium supplementation in older adults with insomnia significantly improved sleep onset time, sleep duration, early morning awakening, and insomnia severity scores compared to placebo over eight weeks. Objective sleep measures including sleep efficiency and serum melatonin levels also improved.

The Deficiency Problem

The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements estimates that approximately 48% of Americans consume less magnesium than the recommended daily amount. Deficiency is exacerbated by chronic stress (which depletes magnesium), high sugar intake, alcohol consumption, and several common medications including proton pump inhibitors and diuretics. Athletes and highly physically active individuals deplete magnesium faster through sweat loss.

The standard symptom list for magnesium deficiency includes muscle cramps, anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbance — a cluster that describes a large portion of people who report poor sleep quality. Many people supplementing with melatonin for sleep problems may be deficient in magnesium and would respond better to addressing that deficiency directly.

Which Form of Magnesium for Sleep

This is where most general advice falls short. Magnesium supplements vary significantly in bioavailability and neurological effect by form:

Magnesium glycinate: The preferred form for sleep and anxiety. Glycine — the amino acid it is bound to — is itself a calming neurotransmitter with independent sleep-supportive properties. Research in Sleep and Biological Rhythms found that glycine supplementation alone improved sleep quality scores and reduced fatigue in subjects with self-reported poor sleep. Magnesium glycinate combines the GABA-activating properties of magnesium with the calming and core-temperature-lowering effects of glycine. High bioavailability, low gastrointestinal side effects.

Magnesium threonate (MgT): The only form demonstrated to cross the blood-brain barrier in meaningful concentrations. Specifically studied for cognitive function and sleep quality. Higher cost, but the best option if brain-level effects are the goal. Research in Nutrients found MgT improved sleep quality in middle-aged adults with subjective sleep complaints.

Magnesium oxide: The most common and cheapest form. Poorest bioavailability — approximately 4% absorbed. Functions primarily as a laxative. Not recommended for sleep support.

Magnesium citrate: Better bioavailability than oxide. More bioavailable than oxide, less so than glycinate. May cause loose stools at higher doses. Reasonable middle option.

Recommended dose for sleep: 200–400mg magnesium glycinate or threonate, taken 30–60 minutes before bed.

What Magnesium Cannot Do

Magnesium addresses a specific pathway — GABAergic inhibition and nervous system calming. It does not address sleep apnea, circadian misalignment, elevated cortisol from chronic stress, or the environmental factors that disrupt sleep architecture. A person sleeping on a heat-trapping mattress that off-gasses compounds keeping their nervous system partially activated will notice limited benefit from magnesium supplementation — because the supplement is working to calm a system that the environment is simultaneously stimulating.

The full picture requires both. Magnesium supports the nervous system's ability to downshift. The sleep environment determines whether that downshift can complete. The Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze — organic natural latex, organic wool temperature regulation, no chemical off-gassing — provides the environmental foundation that makes magnesium's effects more fully expressed. Supplement to the ceiling the environment permits. Then raise the ceiling.

Ask most people what temperature they keep their bedroom and they'll tell you whatever feels comfortable. The problem? What feels comfortable when you're awake is almost never what your brain needs to fall into deep, restorative sleep.

What the Research Actually Says

According to research from the Sleep Foundation, the optimal sleep temperature for most adults falls between 65 and 68°F (18–20°C). That range is cooler than most people keep their homes — and there's a hard biological reason for it.

Your core body temperature needs to drop by approximately 1–2°F to initiate sleep. This isn't a preference. It's a trigger. The hypothalamus — the part of your brain that regulates both temperature and sleep — uses that drop as a cue to release melatonin and begin the transition into deep NREM sleep stages. When your environment is too warm, that drop either doesn't happen fully or happens too slowly, and the signal to enter deep sleep is blunted.

A landmark study in the journal Sleep Medicine Reviews found that thermal environment is one of the most critical factors in sleep onset latency and the amount of slow-wave deep sleep achieved. Put simply: a room that's too warm doesn't just make you uncomfortable. It reduces the quality of your most restorative sleep stages.

But Your Thermostat Is Only Half the Equation

Here's what most people miss: even if your room is the perfect 66°F, your mattress can undo all of it.

Conventional mattresses — especially those made with memory foam and synthetic materials — trap and retain heat at the surface closest to your body. Your thermostat can read 65°F and your body can still be sleeping in a microclimate of 72°F or warmer. That's the temperature that matters. That's the one your brain is responding to.

This is why the materials your mattress and bedding are made from aren't a luxury consideration — they're a functional one.

How The Ultimate Snooze Approaches Temperature

At The Ultimate Snooze, we build every sleep surface around organic temperature regulation.

Our Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze uses certified organic wool as a primary comfort layer. Wool is one of nature's most effective temperature regulators — it actively wicks moisture and draws body heat away from your core, keeping the sleep surface cooler without refrigeration. Unlike synthetic foams that trap heat in their cell structure, organic latex breathes and adapts, maintaining a more neutral surface temperature throughout the night.

Our Breezeline cooling sheet collection extends that regulation to your top layer:

  • Breezeline Air (100% Organic Cotton) — Light, breathable, rated 3/10 for cooling. Ideal for cooler sleepers.
  • Breezeline Comfort (45% Organic Cotton / 55% Natural Linen) — A balanced blend, rated 5/10 for cooling.
  • Breezeline Cool (100% Natural Linen) — Maximum airflow, rated 8/10 for cooling. The choice for hot sleepers.

A Simple Fix That Changes Everything

If you're waking up hot, sweating through the night, or struggling to fall asleep, the fix might not be your thermostat. It might be what you're sleeping on and under.

Set your room to 65–67°F. Switch to an organic mattress and natural fiber sheets. Give your biology the temperature drop it's been waiting for — and watch what happens to your sleep. Explore the Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze.

A year ago, if you told someone you were taping your mouth shut to sleep better, they would have laughed. Now it's one of the most searched sleep topics on the internet — and for good reason. The biology behind it is real.

Why Nasal Breathing During Sleep Matters

Your nose is not just an air passage. It's a biological filter and conditioning system. When you breathe through your nose, air is warmed, humidified, and filtered before it reaches your lungs. More importantly, nasal breathing produces nitric oxide — a vasodilating molecule that improves oxygen delivery to your cells and helps regulate blood pressure.

Research published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine confirmed that nitric oxide — produced in the sinuses and released with nasal breathing — plays a critical role in pulmonary function and cardiovascular health. Mouth breathing bypasses this system entirely.

James Nestor, author of the landmark book Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art, documented through extensive research that chronic mouth breathing is linked to sleep-disordered breathing, elevated cortisol, poor sleep quality, and a host of secondary health consequences. His conclusion: how you breathe during sleep may matter as much as how long you sleep.

What Gary Brecka Says About Nasal Breathing

Gary Brecka has been one of the most prominent voices connecting nasal breathing to recovery, hormonal regulation, and sleep quality. His position aligns with the growing body of research: mouth breathing during sleep increases sleep apnea events, elevates nighttime cortisol, suppresses deep sleep, and reduces the body's ability to fully enter recovery mode.

The fix, in his framework, starts with nasal breathing — and mouth tape is simply the mechanical tool that enforces it while you sleep, before the habit becomes automatic.

Does Mouth Taping Actually Work?

The emerging research suggests yes — with caveats.

A 2022 study published in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine found that mouth taping reduced snoring and mild sleep apnea events in participants, and improved overall sleep quality scores. The mechanism is straightforward: keeping the mouth closed during sleep encourages nasal airflow, reduces apnea events, and maintains better oxygen saturation throughout the night.

The caveat: if you have significant nasal obstruction, mouth taping can backfire. Always consult a doctor before beginning if you suspect any nasal structural issues or undiagnosed sleep apnea.

The Role of Your Sleep Surface in Nasal Breathing

Here's what the mouth taping conversation usually misses: your pillow and mattress directly affect your ability to nasal breathe during sleep.

Proper spinal and cervical alignment — the position of your neck and head relative to your spine — determines whether your airway stays open or partially collapsed during sleep. A pillow that's too high or too flat tilts your head in a way that constricts airflow and makes mouth breathing more likely, even with tape on.

At The Ultimate Snooze, our organic pillow collection is designed with alignment in mind. The Kloud, Organic Snooze Dual, and Signature Cotton pillows each support neutral cervical positioning so your airway stays open — making nasal breathing easier whether you tape or not.

Pair that with the Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze — which supports full spinal alignment and reduces positional shifting during sleep — and you've removed the structural barriers that force the airway compensation in the first place.

Mouth tape is a tool. But the environment around you determines how well that tool can actually work. Build the foundation first — explore our organic pillows.

Some people wake up at 5am feeling ready to conquer the world. Others do not fully come online until 10am and do their best thinking at midnight. This is not laziness or discipline. It is biology. And it has a name: your chronotype.

What a Chronotype Is

Your chronotype is your biological preference for sleep and wake timing, driven by a combination of genetics, age, and environmental factors. It determines when your cortisol peaks in the morning, when your core body temperature reaches its daily high, when melatonin begins rising in the evening, and when your cognitive and physical performance peaks.

Dr. Michael Breus, a clinical psychologist and sleep specialist known as the Sleep Doctor, describes four main chronotype categories: Lions (early risers, peak in the morning), Bears (middle-aligned, the largest group), Wolves (late risers, evening-dominant), and Dolphins (light, irregular sleepers). The Sleep Foundation notes that chronotypes are partly genetic but significantly modifiable by environment and behavior.

The Problem: Most Environments Fight Your Chronotype

Here is what most people do not realize: your chronotype exists on a spectrum, and modern life is systematically pushing nearly everyone toward later sleep timing. Artificial light at night suppresses melatonin and delays your biological sleep signal. Blue light exposure from screens keeps your brain in a state of perceived daytime. Irregular sleep schedules scramble your circadian clock. Research published in Current Biology found that just one week of camping without artificial light significantly shifted participants toward earlier sleep and wake times, suggesting that late chronotypes are partly a product of artificial light exposure rather than pure genetics.

Before you decide you are a permanent night owl, consider how much of your late timing is biology and how much is environment.

How to Work With Your Chronotype

The most powerful lever for shifting or optimizing your chronotype is consistent light exposure. Get bright natural light within 30 minutes of waking to anchor your cortisol peak and signal the start of your biological day. Dim all artificial light two hours before your target sleep time to allow melatonin to rise on schedule. Keep your wake time consistent even on weekends to avoid the social jet lag that compounds chronotype misalignment.

The Role of Your Sleep Surface in Chronotype Optimization

Your chronotype determines when you sleep best. But your sleep surface determines the quality of that sleep once you get there. If you are a Wolf chronotype getting to bed at midnight, you need your sleep environment to be optimized from the moment you lie down so that your shortened sleep window is as restorative as possible.

The Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze and our Breezeline organic sheets are built to maximize the quality of whatever sleep window you have. Organic wool regulates temperature. Organic latex eliminates the pressure points that fragment deep sleep. No synthetic materials means no off-gassing disrupting the nervous system during your most limited and valuable sleep hours.

Know your chronotype. Protect your environment. And make every hour count. Explore the Organic Mattress by Ultimate Snooze.

Is a California King the biggest mattress you can buy? No — but the real question is whether you actually need something bigger, or just something smarter.

This is one of the most searched mattress questions, and the answer changes depending on what problem you are actually trying to solve.

A Quick Reminder on King vs California King

Before talking about what is bigger, it helps to clear up a common misconception.

Standard King: 76 inches wide by 80 inches long

California King: 72 inches wide by 84 inches long

The California King is narrower and longer. Total surface area is almost identical. It is not a bigger mattress — it is a different shape.

Mattresses That Are Actually Bigger Than a California King

Yes, they exist. But they are not what most people are looking for.

Wyoming King: 84 inches by 84 inches

Texas King: 80 inches by 98 inches

Alaskan King: 108 inches by 108 inches

These are specialty or custom-order products. They require custom bed frames, custom sheets, and specialized delivery. They are not widely available and significantly more expensive. For most households they are impractical.

If you are shopping for more room because you share a bed and want more space — there is a more practical solution most people overlook.

The Better Answer for Most Couples: Split King

A Split King is two Twin XL mattresses placed side by side.

Each Twin XL is 38 inches wide by 80 inches long. Together they create a 76-by-80-inch sleeping surface — the same footprint as a standard King.

But each side operates independently.

With a Split King on an adjustable base, each person controls their own head and foot incline. One partner can elevate for reading while the other stays flat. One can use zero-gravity position while the other lies level. There is no compromise because there is no shared adjustment.

For couples with different sleep needs — different firmness preferences, different positions, different schedules — a Split King is often a better solution than simply going bigger.

What You Can Do on a Split King That You Cannot on a Single Mattress

  • Each person adjusts head and foot incline independently
  • Zero motion transfer — one person getting up does not disturb the other
  • Different mattress feel on each side if needed
  • Individual sleep positions throughout the night

The Ultimate Snooze Split King Options

Both the Core™ Bundle and Elite™ Bundle are available in Split King configuration, pairing organic latex mattresses with an adjustable base built for independent movement on each side.

The Core™ Bundle includes the Pure Organic Latex Mattress (Medium Firm) with the 3.0 Adjustable Base.

The Elite™ Bundle includes the Recovery Organic Latex Mattress (Medium feel) with the 5.0 Adjustable Base — the full premium experience with advanced comfort settings.

Both use organic cotton, organic wool, and natural latex designed for long-term recovery and sleep performance.

Explore Split King bundles at The Ultimate Snooze →

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a California King bigger than a King?
No. It is longer (84 vs 80 inches) but narrower (72 vs 76 inches). Total area is nearly the same.

What is the biggest mattress available?
The Alaskan King at 108 by 108 inches is the largest specialty size. Wyoming King (84x84) and Texas King (80x98) also qualify. These require custom frames and bedding.

What is a Split King?
Two Twin XL mattresses (38x80 each) placed side by side — same King footprint, but each side moves independently on its own adjustable base.

Is a Split King the same size as a regular King?
Same overall footprint (76x80). The difference is two independent surfaces instead of one.

Does The Ultimate Snooze offer Split King?
Yes. Both the Core™ and Elite™ bundles are available in Split King.

Final Thought

If you want more room in bed, the answer is not an impractical custom mattress. It is a Split King setup that eliminates compromise — giving each person their own surface, their own position, and their own sleep experience. That is where the real upgrade is.
